page: Microsoft Azure F16-8ams_v7 is a constrained-core virtual machine configuration designed for workloads requiring a substantial memory footprint paired with dedicated single-thread processing capabilities. Operating on Microsoft Hyper-V, the instance features an x86_64 AMD EPYC 9V45 processor clocked at up to 4.5 GHz. It provides 8 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs without simultaneous multithreading (1 thread per core), supplemented by 48 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of L3 cache. Modern vector and cryptographic execution extensions are enabled, including AVX-512, AVX-512 VNNI, AVX-512 BF16, and AES.

Despite its 8-core allocation, the instance delivers 128.0 GB of system memory, translating to a high ratio of 16.0 GB per core. The machine contains no GPUs and includes no local temporary storage, requiring external Azure storage volumes for persistence and operating system disks. Hardware benchmarks demonstrate exceptional single-core processing capabilities, with stress-ng single-core compute, single-threaded gzip compression, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression all landing in the top 10% of results. Memory evaluation shows strong performance in PassMark memory tests, accompanied by large-block uncached read and write bandwidths of 53.9 GB/sec and 34.05 GB/sec.

Resource-density tradeoffs reflect its constrained vCPU profile. Multi-core compute benchmarks, PassMark database operations, and multi-threaded decompression tests fall into the median range due to the 8-thread ceiling. Inference benchmarks show strong throughput on small language models—exceeding 389 tokens per second for text generation on a 135M model—but diminish significantly on 70B parameter models due to the absence of dedicated GPU accelerators and memory bandwidth constraints relative to massive model requirements.

By restricting active compute cores while maintaining a large 128 GB memory allocation, the F16-8ams_v7 provides strong cost efficiency for software environments licensed per core, such as enterprise databases and commercial middleware. It is well matched for memory-intensive caching layers, in-memory databases, lightweight AI inference, data compression pipelines, and general enterprise workloads requiring substantial RAM without paying for unused CPU capacity.
